ref: 1 Apol. 6 (New Advent/ANF chapter numbering; Otto 1842 chapter 6)
greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἐκεῖνον τε, καὶ τὸν παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ υἱὸν ἐλθόντα καὶ διδάξαντα ἡμᾶς ταῦτα, καὶ τὸν τῶν ἄλλων ἑπομένων καὶ ἐξομοιουμένων ἀγαθῶν ἀγγέλων στρατόν, πνεῦμά τε τὸ προφητικὸν σεβόμεθα καὶ προσκυνοῦμεν, λόγῳ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ τιμῶντες
greek_edition: J.C.T. Otto, S. Justini philosophi et martyris opera, vol. 1 (Jena 1842), archive.org item bib_fict_4102644_1. Read from the OCR text layer (djvu and PDF); Latin apparatus is interleaved on the page, so the Greek was assembled from the clean lines. Printed page 148 (PDF p.228) to 150 (PDF p.230); the OCR reads '199' for the p.150 running head, which I take as an OCR error (inferred from the 148/149 sequence).
english: “But both Him, and the Son (who came forth from Him and taught us these things, and the host of the other good angels who follow and are made like to Him), and the prophetic Spirit, we worship and adore, knowing them in reason and truth, and declaring without grudging to every one who wishes to learn, as we have been taught.”
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Otto, Jena 1842 (vol. 1); ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885 (New Advent)
what_it_says: Christians worship the Father, the Son who came from Him, and the prophetic Spirit, listed together as objects of worship.
limits: The Son and the Spirit are named after the Father with no statement of their relation to one another; the Spirit is 'prophetic', which is a functional description. The Greek clause is OCR with one uncertain word (ἐκεῖνον).

greek: Ὄντως θεοῦ μανθάνοντες καὶ ἐν δευτέρᾳ χώρᾳ ἔχοντες, πνεῦμά τε τὸ προφητικὸν ἐν τρίτῃ τάξει, ὅτι “μετὰ λόγου τιμῶμεν”, ἀποθείξομεν.
greek_edition: J.C.T. Otto, S. Justini ... opera, vol. 1 (Jena 1842), archive.org bib_fict_4102644_1, OCR text layer. The scan prints 'ἀποδείξομεν' as 'ἀποθείξομεν' in OCR; the sentence is split across lines with a Latin note interleaved. Printed page 164 (PDF p.244).
english: “that we reasonably worship Him, having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third, we will prove.”
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
page: Otto 1842: p. 164 (printed; running head on PDF p.244)
what_it_says: Justin says the Christian worships the Son in the second place and the prophetic Spirit in the third, i.e. an ordered sequence of three.
limits: This is an ordering (second place, third rank) and does not say the Spirit is a distinct person in the sense of Nicene homoousios. The OCR of the accents is imperfect. The same passage gives the Son as the one 'of the true God', which is the Logos-as-Son reading.

greek: Ἡ δὲ πρώτη δύναμις μετὰ τὸν πατέρα πάντων καὶ δεσπότην θεὸν καὶ υἱὸς ὁ λόγος ἐστίν, ὃς τίνα τρόπον σαρκοποιηθεὶς ἄνθρωπος γέγονεν, ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς ἐροῦμεν.
greek_edition: J.C.T. Otto, S. Justini ... opera, vol. 1 (Jena 1842), archive.org bib_fict_4102644_1, OCR. The OCR has a stray 'ri' after 'πάντων' and a split line; the clause 'ἡ δὲ πρώτη δύναμις ... υἱὸς ὁ λόγος ἐστίν' is clear. PDF p.286.
english: “And the first power after God the Father and Lord of all is the Word, who is also the Son; and of Him we will, in what follows, relate how He took flesh and became man.”
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
page: Otto 1842: p. 206 inferred (OCR running head reads '900'; neighbours on PDF pp.284-285 read 204 and 205)
what_it_says: Justin calls the Word the first power after the Father and Lord of all, and says the Word is also the Son.
limits: 'First power' (δύναμις) is the same word Justin uses for the Word as the Father's power in Dialogue 128, so the phrase is a power-language not a person-language. The printed page is inferred, not read.

greek: λόγον ὄντα, οὗ πᾶν γένος ἀνθρώπων μετέσχε. Καὶ οἳ μετὰ λόγου βιώσαντες Χριστιανοί εἶσι, κἂν ἄθεοι ἐνομίσθησαν
greek_edition: J.C.T. Otto, S. Justini ... opera, vol. 1 (Jena 1842), archive.org bib_fict_4102644_1, OCR. The clause 'Χριστὸν πρωτότοκον τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι ἐδιδάχθημεν καὶ προεμηνύσαμεν' precedes it in the same chapter (OCR read; I did not confirm its PDF page). PDF p.310 (printed 230).
english: “We have been taught that Christ is the first-born of God, and we have declared above that He is the Word of whom every race of men were partakers; and those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists.”
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: Justin says the Word is the first-born of God and that every race of men has shared in the Word, which is why reasonable pre-Christian people count as Christians.
limits: This is about the Word's presence in reasonable people, not about the Spirit or a three-part scheme. The 'Word before Christ' motif is the context that explains why Justin can speak of the Word as a universal reason.

greek_edition: Not located. The Greek of 2 Apol. 6 was searched in the Otto 1842 OCR (archive.org bib_fict_4102644_1) for 'πρὸ τῶν ἔργων', 'πρὸ τῶν ἔργων γεννηθείς' and related forms without a hit. Not verified.
english: “And His Son, who alone is properly called Son, the Word who also was with Him and was begotten before the works, when at first He created and arranged all things by Him, is called Christ.”
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
page: page unknown (chapter 6 of the Second Apology)
what_it_says: The Son is 'the Word who was with' God and 'begotten before the works', through whom all things were created.
limits: 'Begotten before the works' is the same generation-before-creation language as Theophilus 2.10; it does not mention the Spirit. The Greek has not been checked.

greek: γεγέννηκε δύναμίν τινα ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ λογικήν, ἥτις καὶ δόξα κυρίου ὑπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ ἁγίου καλεῖται, ποτὲ δὲ υἱὸς, ποτὲ δὲ σοφία
greek_edition: J.C.T. Otto, S. Justini ... opera, vol. 2 (Jena 1843), archive.org bib_fict_4102644_2, OCR text layer only. Its PDF is 70 MB, over the 60 MB limit, so it was not downloaded. The Greek is read from the OCR with the apparatus interleaved; the word 'ἐξ' and the opening of the chapter are clear.
english: “God begot before all creatures a Beginning, [who was] a certain rational power [proceeding] from Himself, who is called by the Holy Spirit, now the Glory of the Lord, now the Son, again Wisdom, again an Angel, then God, and then Lord and Logos.”
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: God begot a rational power from Himself before creation, which the Holy Spirit names by several titles: Glory of the Lord, Son, Wisdom, Angel, God and Logos.
limits: Justin's own words here name the Holy Spirit as the speaker of the titles, not as a distinct person begotten; the names are interchangeable (Son, Wisdom, Angel), which is the same looseness Theophilus shows. The 'begets the word' comparison (human speech, fire from fire) is an analogy.

greek: [ὄντως] ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς προβληθὲν γέννημα πρὸ πάντων τῶν ποιημάτων συνῆν τῷ πατρί, καὶ τούτῳ ὁ πατὴρ ὁμιλεῖ
greek_edition: J.C.T. Otto, S. Justini ... opera, vol. 2 (Jena 1843), archive.org bib_fict_4102644_2, OCR only. The OCR is damaged ('τῷ ovtt', 'προβ}ληϑὲν'); the bracketed word is my reading of the OCR, not a confirmed one. Interleaved apparatus.
english: “But this Offspring, which was truly brought forth from the Father, was with the Father before all the creatures, and the Father communed with Him.”
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: The Offspring brought forth from the Father was with the Father before all creatures and the Father conversed with it.
limits: The language of 'Offspring brought forth' (γέννημα, προβληθέν) is generation-by-procession, which is the Stoic-flavoured model the objection targets. Justin says 'Father communed with Him' with no Spirit clause in this sentence.

ref: Dial. 128 (quoted in Otto's note to c. 61)
greek: τὴν δύναμιν ταύτην γεγεννῆσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρός, δυνάμει καὶ βουλῇ αὐτοῦ, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ κατὰ ἀποτομήν, ὡς ἀπομεριζομένης τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς οὐσίας
greek_edition: Greek taken from Otto's critical note to c. 61 in archive.org bib_fict_4102644_2 (Otto 1843 vol. 2), where Otto quotes Justin's c. 128 text. The Greek of c. 128 itself was not read in the main text. OCR only.
english: “this power was begotten from the Father, by His power and will, but not by abscission, as if the essence of the Father were divided”
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1), Dial. 128 text read at New Advent 01289.htm
page: page unknown (Otto 1843 vol. 2, note on c. 61; Otto cites c. 128)
what_it_says: Justin says the power is begotten from the Father by the Father's power and will, not by cutting off a part of the Father's substance.
limits: This is the key defence of Justin's generation language against the 'division' objection. It answers division, not the 'point of time' problem: the 'will' clause still makes the begetting an act at a moment.

ref: Or. 5 (Tatian, Address to the Greeks, chapter 5)
greek: Θελήματι δὲ τῆς ἁπλότητος αὐτοῦ προπηδᾷ λόγος· ὁ δὲ λόγος, οὐ κατὰ κενοῦ χωρήσας, ἔργον πρωτότοκον τοῦ πατρὸς γίνεται.
greek_edition: Otto's Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum (Tatian text), reprinted 1969, archive.org bib_fict_4102644 -> item corpusapologeta03moragoog (OCR). The volume number of Otto's Tatian text is not confirmed. The reprint's PDF has no text layer, so no PDF page could be checked.
english: “And by His simple will the Logos springs forth; and the Logos, not coming forth in vain, becomes the first-begotten work of the Father.”
edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum (Tatian), reprint 1969; ANF vol. 2, Buffalo 1885
what_it_says: By the Father's simple will the Logos 'springs forth' and becomes the first-begotten work of the Father, and the Logos that comes forth does not diminish the Logos-power in the Father.
limits: Tatian uses 'springs forth' (προπηδᾷ) and 'first-begotten work' (ἔργον πρωτότοκον), not Justin's ἐνδιάθετος/προφορικός. He says the Logos is a 'work' of the Father, which an Arian can cite as creaturely. The apologist's torch analogy also shows the Logos as distinct from the Father in a derivative way.

greek: τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέῳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ· πρὸς αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ. Ὄντος δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐν πατρὶ καὶ πατρὸς ἐν υἱῷ, ἑνότητι καὶ δυνάμει πνεύματος, νοῦς καὶ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.
greek_edition: J.C.T. Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis opera (Jena 1857), archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe, OCR text layer. The initial article of the Greek is lost in the OCR (the line starts 'τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος'), and 'Ὄντος' is printed 'Ovrog'. PDF p.130; printed page not read from the scan.
english: “But the Son of God is the Logos of the Father, in idea and in operation; for after the pattern of Him and by Him were all things made, the Father and the Son being one. And, the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son, in oneness and power of spirit, the understanding and reason of the Father is the Son of God.”
what_it_says: The Son is the Logos of the Father in idea and operation; the Father and Son are one, each in the other, in oneness of spirit (power), and the Son is the Father's understanding and reason.
limits: 'Power of spirit' (δυνάμει πνεύματος) is not the Holy Spirit as a person; this sentence has no third person. The Logos is equated with the Father's nous and logos, which is a Logos-as-faculty model (the Theophilus pattern). Athenagoras ch.10 is the chapter the brief calls ch.12: ch.12 in ANF is headed 'The Two Kinds of Spirits' and is not Trinitarian.

ref: Leg. 10 (Athenagoras, chapter 10): Father, Son and Holy Spirit named together
greek: Τίς οὖν οὐκ ἂν ἀπορήσαι, λέγοντας θεὸν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν θεὸν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, δεικνύντας αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει δύναμιν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ τάξει διαίρεσιν, ἀκούσας ἀθέους καλουμένους; (and, in the main text, πνεῦμα ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμὲν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον ὡς ἀκτῖνα)
greek_edition: Otto 1857 (athenagoraephilo00athe), OCR. The first sentence is quoted in Otto's note as 'Provoco ad verba c. 10'; the 'ἀπόῤῥοια' clause is in the main text (PDF p.132). The note's wording is Otto's citation of the text, so it is PARTLY. Printed page not read.
english: “Who, then, would not be astonished to hear men who speak of God the Father, and of God the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and who declare both their power in union and their distinction in order, called atheists?” and: “The Holy Spirit Himself also, which operates in the prophets, we assert to be an effluence of God, flowing from Him, and returning back again like a beam of the sun.”
what_it_says: Athenagoras names God the Father, God the Son and the Holy Spirit together, claims the Father and Son are one in power and distinct in order, and calls the Spirit an effluence of God like a sunbeam.
limits: The 'union in power, distinction in order' formula is the closest Apologist match to a Nicene-style Trinity, but 'effluence' (ἀπόῤῥοια) is an emanation image and does not by itself make the Spirit a separate person in the homoousios sense. The English heading 'Father, Son, and Holy Ghost' is the ANF translator's, not Athenagoras's text.

greek: Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit; ... quasi ipse suas non haberet manus.
greek_edition: Latin, not Greek (Book IV survives only in Latin, apart from fragments). Harvey's edition, Sancti Irenaei ... libros quinque adversus haereses (Cambridge 1857), archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog, OCR. The Harvey PDF has no text layer, so the page cannot be checked and the printed page is not read.
english: “...as if He did not possess His own hands. For with Him were always present the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, by whom and in whom, freely and spontaneously, He made all things...”
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: God made all things through the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, who are always with Him, so that He does not need His 'hands' (angels or other powers).
limits: The Latin is the only text of this sentence; there is no Greek, and the 'hands' image is a figure, not a distinct ontology. The sentence gives the 'Wisdom' and 'Spirit' pairing that the Theophilus issue turns on, and does not resolve whether Wisdom and Spirit are distinct persons.

greek: Et quoniam Verbum, id est Filius, semper cum Patre erat, per multa demonstravimus. Quoniam autem et Sapientia, quae est Spiritus, erat apud eum ante omnem constitutionem
greek_edition: Latin, not Greek. Harvey 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog), OCR; no PDF text layer, so no page check.
english: “I have also largely demonstrated, that the Word, namely the Son, was always with the Father; and that Wisdom also, which is the Spirit, was present with Him, anterior to all creation.”
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: Irenaeus identifies the Word with the Son and Wisdom with the Spirit, and says both were with God before creation.
limits: This is the exact identification the brief's point (3) is about: 'Wisdom, which is the Spirit'. It is an identification of two names with two persons, so an Arian or Unitarian can read it as Wisdom=Spirit=a single created or semi-divine agent, and a Trinitarian can read it as 'Wisdom' being the Holy Spirit, distinct from the Son.

greek_edition: Not located. Searched archive.org Bonwetsch volumes hippolytuswerk01hipp, hippolytuswerke01hipp, hippolytuswerke02hipp (no CN text found) and the Elenchos volume (see U10-15). The 1977 'contranoetum0000hipp' is a modern edition and was not read.
english: “And as the Author, and fellow-Counsellor, and Framer of the things that are in formation, He begot the Word; and as He bears this Word in Himself ... uttering the voice first, and begetting Him as Light of Light, He set Him forth to the world as its Lord, (and) His own mind.”
what_it_says: God begets the Word, then utters ('makes visible') the Word as Light of Light, making it the Son and the Father's own mind.
limits: The English is clearly the endiathetos/prophorikos schema, but the translator does not use the Greek terms and the Greek of CN 10 was not located, so the terms are not attested here. The schema is also modalist in CN's own sense (the Word is 'made visible' in the world), which Hippolytus is refuting, not endorsing.

greek: Οὗτος οὖν μόνος καὶ κατὰ πάντων ϑεὸς λόγον πρῶτον ἐννοηϑεὶς ἀπογεννᾷ, οὐ λόγον ὡς φωνήν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐνδιάϑετον τοῦ παντὸς λογισμόν. τοῦτον μόνον ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐγέννα· ... φωνὴν εἶχεν ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὰς ἐν τῷ πατρὶ προεννοηϑείσας ἰδέας
greek_edition: Hippolytus Werke vol. 3 (archive.org hippolytuswerke03hipp; metadata: 1897, G.N. Bonwetsch), Elenchos X text, PDF text layer (PDF p.317). The Greek is clean on this page. Running head 'Elenchos X 31, 6-23, 7' and printed page 289. This is the Refutatio, not Contra Noetum.
edition: Hippolytus Werke vol. 3 (Bonwetsch, 1897 as catalogued); Greek only
what_it_says: A teaching Hippolytus describes and refutes has God first conceive a Logos and beget it as 'endiathetos' (immanent reason of the whole), not as a voice; the begotten one then 'has a voice' (φωνὴν) in itself, the Ideas from the Father's mind.
limits: This is Hippolytus describing a rival teaching (the Refutatio is polemic); the group is not identified in my reading, so do not attribute it to Hippolytus or to Theophilus without checking the X.33 heading. The sentence is the earliest Greek pairing of endiathetos with the begetting; it is not Theophilus's own term.

greek: ante omnia enim deus erat solus ... habebat enim secum quam habebat in semetipso, rationem suam scilicet. rationalis enim deus, et ratio in ipsum prius et ita ab ipso omnia. quae ratio sensus ipsius est, hanc Graeci λόγον dicunt, quo uocabulo etiam sermonem appellamus ... nam etsi deus nondum sermonem suum miserat, proinde eum cum ipsa et in ipsa ratione intra semetipsum habebat
greek_edition: Latin (not Greek): Kroymann, Q. Septimii Florentis Tertulliani opera, pars II, CSEL 47 (Vienna 1906), archive.org quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft; PDF text layer read at PDF p.273. The Greek word is λόγον as printed in the Latin text.
english: “For God is rational, and Reason was first in Him ... God had not Word from the beginning, but He had Reason even before the beginning ... although God had not yet sent out His Word, He still had Him within Himself.”
what_it_says: Before creation God had Reason in Himself, which the Greeks call Logos; the Word is that reason sent out later, so the Word was 'within' God before it was 'sent forth'.
limits: Tertullian is the Latin version of the immanent/uttered distinction, the Logos-within-God-then-sent-out pattern. He says God had Reason before the beginning but did not have the sent-out Word from the beginning; this is the same timing tension that Theophilus's 'begotten' language raises. The Latin uses 'ratio/sermo', not endiathetos/prophorikos.

greek: secundus autem ubi est, duo sunt, et tertius ubi est, tres sunt. tertius enim est spiritus a deo et filio, sicut tertius a radice fructus ex frutice et tertius
greek_edition: Latin (not Greek): Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), PDF text layer read at PDF p.279 (CSEL p.239). OCR of the text printed 'siout' for 'sicut'.
english: “Where, however, there is a second, there must be two; and where there is a third, there must be three. Now the Spirit indeed is third from God and the Son; just as the fruit of the tree is third from the root, or as the stream out of the river is third from the fountain.”
what_it_says: The Spirit is the third, after the Father and the Son, as a fruit is third from the root and a stream is third from the fountain.
limits: This is the clearest Latin statement of three ordered persons (tertius = Spirit), which is what the brief asks for. But it is an analogy of derivation ('from God and the Son'), so it says the Spirit proceeds from both, and it says nothing about homoousios.

ref: De princ. 1.2 (ANF Book I, chapter 2, section 3; Görgemanns-Karpp 1.2.2)
greek_edition: Not located. Only the English was read; no Greek or Latin of De principiis 1.2.2 was checked.
english: “Now, in the same way in which we have understood that Wisdom was the beginning of the ways of God, and is said to be created ... must we understand her to be the Word of God, because of her disclosing to all other beings ... the nature of the mysteries and secrets which are contained within the divine wisdom.”
page: ANF Book I ch.2 sect.3 (no printed page)
what_it_says: Origen identifies Wisdom with the Word, on the ground that Wisdom reveals the hidden things of God, and says it is impious to deny that the unbegotten Father always had generated the Word and possessed Wisdom.
limits: No Holy Spirit is named in this passage, so it does not answer Theophilus point (3). No endiathetos/prophorikos language was seen in the English I read; that is a negative result for ch.2 only, not for the whole of Origen.
